2.lead: The verse states that all praise belongs to Allah. The phrase All praise is for Allah places praise at the start of the reader's words after the opening name. The word all means that no part of praise is kept back from Him, so whatever good the reader sees has its source in Allah. The phrase Lord of all worlds names Allah in His role as the one who nurtures and manages everything that exists. The word Lord points to care that brings a thing from its beginning toward its perfection, and the word worlds covers everything that exists, not only the human world. Together the two phrases link praise to a view of the whole universe. The one who praises Allah recognises that Allah alone is the source of every order, and that He is the one who sustains it. The verse follows the opening name in the first verse. Having named Allah with mercy, the reader now gives Him praise, since mercy is a reason for thanks. The next verse returns to the qualities of mercy, so the reader moves from praise to a closer view of the Lord of all worlds, who is also the Most Compassionate and the Most Merciful. This verse is the first step in the movement of the surah from the name, to praise, and then to worship and request. A reader who keeps the first verse in mind hears this verse as praise given for a mercy already named.

3.lead: The verse repeats two names of Allah, the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful. The phrase the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful has two parts, one for a mercy that covers all creation and one for a mercy given most fully to believers. The verse is placed directly after the praise in the previous verse. Having named the Lord of all worlds as the one who gives praise its meaning, the surah now describes that Lord by the qualities of His mercy. The reader learns that the Lord who nurtures every creature is also the one who is merciful to them. The next verse names the Master of the Day of Judgment, so mercy is set beside justice and accountability. A reader who sees the mercy first is reminded that the account on that Day is also carried out by the One who is merciful. The repetition also gives the reader time to dwell on the mercy before moving on to the next name. The reader is asked to hold the two names together, since the first describes a mercy that is shown in the making and sustaining of all things, and the second describes a mercy that is shown in the guidance of believers.

4.lead: The verse describes Allah as the Master of the Day of Judgment. The phrase Master of the Day of Judgment names Allah as the one who has full authority on the Day when every person is repaid for what he did. The word master means the one who has possession and control of a matter, and the Day of Judgment is the Day when that control is seen clearly by all creatures. The verse follows the two names of mercy in the previous verse. The reader is given a balance between mercy and the account, so the mercy of Allah is not a reason to forget that every deed will be weighed. The next verse turns from the Master of that Day to the worship and the request of the servant. Since the Day is named here, the worship in the next verse is made with seriousness, and the prayer for guidance at the end of the surah is made with the Day in view. This verse links the mercy of Allah with His justice and turns the reader's thoughts toward accountability before he speaks to his Lord directly.

5.lead: The verse is addressed directly to Allah, and it turns the reader from praising Him to standing before Him. The phrase You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help has two halves joined by the word and. The first half means that worship is given to Allah and to Him alone. The word alone matters because it removes any other object from the act of worship. The second half means that help is asked from Allah and from Him alone. The reader is not only declaring worship, but also admitting that he cannot finish any task without Allah's help. The two halves come one after the other because worship is the purpose and help is the means that makes worship possible. The verse places You before we in each half. This puts Allah first in the sentence, so the words make clear that the one addressed is the one who deserves the worship. Looking back, the previous verses have named Allah, praised Him, and described His mercy and His authority on the Day of Judgment. This verse answers that description with a response. The reader stops describing and begins to speak to Allah in the first person plural, joining the community of believers. Looking ahead, the next verse asks for guidance on the straight path, and that request depends on the admission made here. A servant who admits that he worships Allah alone and asks Him for help is ready to ask for the right path. The verse is therefore the point where the surah moves from praise to prayer.
